docs.title: Working notes
docs.text:
Notes on Linux internals, Rust, eBPF, and the parts of running infrastructure that only become obvious at 3am. Written while the details are still fresh, which means occasionally being wrong in public and correcting it later.

This is where the reasoning behind the opinions on helius.dk lives. If you want to know how I think before you email me, start here.

docs.title: Blackbox Linux — build notes
docs.text:
Working notes from building Blackbox Linux: an eBPF runtime visibility agent for Linux servers, written in Rust. Process-tree tracing, in-kernel filtering, a small declarative rule engine.

Not released yet

First public release targets December 2026. Until there is a tagged version and a public repository, everything here describes intent and work-in-progress, not shipped behaviour. If you are evaluating it for production, wait for the tag.

This section is the engineering diary — the decisions, the measurements, and the things that turned out to be wrong. The product page has the overview and architecture; this is where the reasoning lives.

docs.title: Why it is being built in the open
docs.text: The claim Blackbox makes is that you should not run an agent you cannot audit as root on every host you own. That claim is only worth anything if the work itself is inspectable — including the parts that did not work. So the notes go up as they happen rather than being tidied into a launch post.

docs.title: What gets written about here
docs.text:
• Kernel work — probe attachment, CO-RE, what verifier rejections actually meant, why a given hook was the wrong one.
  • Filtering — the cost of an event that reaches userspace versus one dropped in-kernel, measured rather than assumed.
  • Correlation — turning a flat stream of fork/execve/exit into process trees a human can read, and where that gets expensive.
  • Overhead — honest numbers on real workloads, including the cases where the overhead was worse than expected.

docs.title: Follow along
docs.text: There is no mailing list. Posts land in the blog, and the repository goes public with the first release. If you have a use case that should shape it — particularly an environment where existing agents were too expensive or too opaque — email me and tell me about it while the design is still soft.

docs.title: Rebuilding helius.dk
docs.text: For a few years helius.dk was a MkDocs blog and nothing else — Solana tooling, Rust performance notes, kernel debugging. It has now grown a front end, because the consulting side needed somewhere to point people that was not a list of posts about ring buffers.

docs.title: What changed
docs.text:
The marketing site is Astro and owns the root domain. The blog is still MkDocs and now lives here at /blog. They are two independent static builds stitched together at deploy time:

mkdocs build -d public/blog   →  Astro copies public/ verbatim
astro build                   →  dist/  →  GitHub Pages

Neither half knows the other exists. That is deliberate: I can rebuild the blog without touching the site, and the site has no content pipeline reaching into Markdown it does not own. The cost is that a broken Python step fails the whole deploy, which is a trade I will take for the isolation.

The old post URLs are gone

The previous blog served posts from the domain root. Those paths now 404 rather than redirect. That was a deliberate call and it does throw away whatever ranking those pages had — if you were linking to one, that link is dead and I am not going to pretend otherwise.

docs.title: What the site is for
docs.text:
Helius does DevOps engineering: CI/CD, Kubernetes, infrastructure as code, observability, Linux hardening, performance work. All of it with open-source tooling, all of it committed to repositories the client owns.

The whole argument is on the pledge page, and it comes down to one test: a month after I stop working with you, is anything degraded? If the answer could be yes, I built the wrong thing.

docs.title: What lands in December
docs.text:
Blackbox Linux — an eBPF runtime visibility agent for Linux servers, written in Rust. Process-tree tracing, in-kernel filtering so uninteresting events never cost you anything, and a small declarative rule engine.

It exists because runtime security on Linux is mostly sold as closed agents licensed per host, and an agent you cannot audit has no business running as root on your servers.

It is not released yet. First public release targets December 2026, and until there is a tagged version, treat everything written about it as intent rather than documentation.

docs.title: Housekeeping
docs.text:
Posts here are in English only. The marketing site is bilingual (English and Danish); the blog is not, because maintaining translated technical writing is a commitment I would rather not make badly.

More to come — mostly eBPF, mostly Rust, occasionally a post-mortem where I was the cause.

docs.title: Snippets
docs.text:
Short things worth writing down once so I stop re-deriving them at 3am. No narrative, no build-up — the command, what it does, and the caveat.

Every snippet is run on a real machine before it goes here, and each page says which versions. Longer reasoning lives in posts.

Category What is in it BPF and kernel tracing bpftrace and ftrace: syscall latency, kernel function calls, call graphs, stacks, failed opens, outgoing connections Kubernetes and containers What a node has reserved, and deploying by digest Network forensics ss, nc, ping, mtr, tcpdump: who listens, who talks, where packets die nftables Load a default-deny ruleset over SSH without locking yourself out PostgreSQL Find the query that costs the most in total strace Which files a service opens, where its time goes, which calls fail systemd Units that really restart, and how exposed each service is

docs.title: BPF and kernel tracing
docs.text:
Live answers from the running kernel: no restart, no recompiling, no agent. All of these need root and exit on their own after a few seconds. bpftrace comes first; ftrace, which needs nothing installed, is at the end.

Tested with bpftrace 0.20.2 on Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 6.8. fentry probes need a kernel with BTF (/sys/kernel/btf/vmlinux exists), which every current major distribution ships.

docs.title: Find what a process is actually waiting on
docs.text:
# Syscall latency histogram (µs) for one PID, for 30 seconds.
sudo bpftrace -e '
  tracepoint:raw_syscalls:sys_enter /pid == '"$PID"'/ {
    @s[tid] = nsecs; @nr[tid] = args->id;
  }
  tracepoint:raw_syscalls:sys_exit  /pid == '"$PID"' && @s[tid]/ {
    @us[@nr[tid]] = hist((nsecs - @s[tid]) / 1000);
    delete(@s[tid]); delete(@nr[tid]);
  }
  interval:s:30 { exit(); }
  END { clear(@s); clear(@nr); }'

Keys are syscall numbers; ausyscall 220 (from auditd) names them, and they differ per architecture. The number is recorded on entry because on arm64 rt_sigreturn reports -1 on exit. The answer is usually one syscall you were not thinking about.

docs.title: Which kernel functions can I trace?
docs.text:
sudo bpftrace -l 'kprobe:tcp_*'          # every traceable function matching tcp_*
sudo bpftrace -lv 'fentry:tcp_connect'   # its typed arguments (needs BTF)

docs.title: Count calls to a family of kernel functions
docs.text:
# Which VFS functions run most over 5 seconds?
sudo bpftrace -e 'kprobe:vfs_* { @[func] = count(); } interval:s:5 { exit(); }'

Keep wildcards narrow. vfs_* is about 80 probes; tcp_* is about 500, and attaching that many takes a while and costs real overhead on a busy host.

docs.title: How long does a kernel function take?
docs.text:
# vfs_read latency (µs), per process, for 10 seconds.
sudo bpftrace -e '
  kprobe:vfs_read { @start[tid] = nsecs; }
  kretprobe:vfs_read /@start[tid]/ {
    @us[comm] = hist((nsecs - @start[tid]) / 1000); delete(@start[tid]);
  }
  interval:s:10 { exit(); }
  END { clear(@start); }'

Swap vfs_read for any function from bpftrace -l. Inlined functions do not appear in the list and cannot be traced this way.

docs.title: Who calls this function?
docs.text:
# Kernel stacks leading into tcp_v4_connect, counted per process.
sudo bpftrace -e 'kprobe:tcp_v4_connect { @[comm, kstack(6)] = count(); } interval:s:10 { exit(); }'

The stack is the fastest way to learn which code path you are actually on before reading kernel source.

docs.title: Which processes fail to open files, and why?
docs.text:
# Failed opens per process and errno (-2 = ENOENT, -13 = EACCES).
sudo bpftrace -e '
  kretprobe:do_sys_openat2 /(int64)retval < 0/ { @[comm, (int64)retval] = count(); }
  interval:s:10 { exit(); }'

With the file names, using typed arguments:

sudo bpftrace -e '
  fexit:do_sys_openat2 /retval < 0/ {
    printf("%-16s %4d %s\n", comm, retval, str(uptr(args->filename)));
  }
  interval:s:10 { exit(); }'

uptr() matters: the file name lives in user memory, and without it the name prints empty.

docs.title: Every outgoing TCP connection, as it happens
docs.text:
# Process, PID and destination of each new IPv4 TCP connection.
sudo bpftrace -e '
  fentry:tcp_connect {
    $sk = args->sk;
    if ($sk->__sk_common.skc_family == 2) {   // AF_INET
      printf("%-16s %-7d -> %s:%d\n", comm, pid,
        ntop($sk->__sk_common.skc_daddr), bswap($sk->__sk_common.skc_dport));
    }
  }
  interval:s:30 { exit(); }'

Good for answering "what is this host talking to?" during an investigation, including connections that close before ss would ever see them. The port is stored in network byte order, hence bswap.

docs.title: ftrace: kernel tracing without BPF
docs.text:
ftrace is built into the kernel and driven by writing to files in /sys/kernel/tracing. Nothing to install, which makes it the tool for hosts where you cannot add bpftrace. Run these from a root shell (sudo -i); each one cleans up after itself. Kernels in lockdown "confidentiality" mode block it.

Tested on kernel 6.8 and trace-cmd 3.2.

docs.title: Every program executed on the host, live
docs.text:
cd /sys/kernel/tracing
echo 1 > events/sched/sched_process_exec/enable
timeout 30 cat trace_pipe
echo 0 > events/sched/sched_process_exec/enable

Catches short-lived processes that ps never shows: the cron job, the curl | sh, the shell an attacker spawns.

docs.title: Call graph with timings for one kernel function
docs.text:
cd /sys/kernel/tracing
echo do_sys_openat2 > set_graph_function
echo 3 > max_graph_depth
echo function_graph > current_tracer
sleep 5
echo 0 > tracing_on      # stop first: changing the tracer wipes the buffer
grep -v '^#' trace | head -40
echo nop > current_tracer; echo 1 > tracing_on
echo > set_graph_function; echo 0 > max_graph_depth

Output reads like code: each child call with its time, and + marks calls over 10 µs. Here it shows that most of an open is spent in path_openat.

docs.title: Hit counts for a family of functions
docs.text:
cd /sys/kernel/tracing
echo 'tcp_*' > set_ftrace_filter
echo 1 > function_profile_enabled
sleep 10
echo 0 > function_profile_enabled
cat trace_stat/function* | awk '$2 ~ /^[0-9]+$/ { hits[$1] += $2 } END { for (f in hits) print hits[f], f }' \
  | sort -nr | head -20
echo > set_ftrace_filter

The profiler keeps one table per CPU; the awk adds them up.

docs.title: Failed opens, with a kretprobe and a filter
docs.text:
cd /sys/kernel/tracing
echo 'r:snip/open_fail do_sys_openat2 ret=$retval:s64' >> dynamic_events
echo 'ret < 0' > events/snip/open_fail/filter
echo 1 > events/snip/open_fail/enable
timeout 10 cat trace_pipe
echo 0 > events/snip/open_fail/enable
echo '-:snip/open_fail' >> dynamic_events

The filter runs in the kernel, so only failures reach the buffer.

docs.title: Function arguments, with a kprobe event
docs.text:
cd /sys/kernel/tracing
echo 'p:snip/open do_sys_openat2 path=+0($arg2):ustring' >> dynamic_events
echo 1 > events/snip/open/enable
timeout 10 cat trace_pipe
echo 0 > events/snip/open/enable
echo '-:snip/open' >> dynamic_events

$arg2 is the second argument, +0(…):ustring reads it as a string from user memory. An occasional path=(fault) is a page not yet in memory, not an error.

docs.title: The same with trace-cmd
docs.text:
trace-cmd wraps all of the above and handles the cleanup. It writes trace.dat to the current directory.

# Call graph of every open made by one command.
sudo trace-cmd record -p function_graph -g do_sys_openat2 --max-graph-depth 3 -F cat /etc/hostname
sudo trace-cmd report | head -40

# Or an already running process and the children it starts (-c).
sudo trace-cmd record -p function_graph -g do_sys_openat2 --max-graph-depth 3 -P "$PID" -c sleep 10
sudo trace-cmd report | less

If a session is interrupted and leaves tracing switched on, sudo trace-cmd reset puts everything back.

docs.title: Kubernetes and containers
docs.text: Tested with kubectl against k3s, and docker buildx 0.29.

docs.title: What is actually eating the node
docs.text:
kubectl get pods -A -o custom-columns=\
'NS:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,'\
'CPU_REQ:.spec.containers[*].resources.requests.cpu,'\
'MEM_REQ:.spec.containers[*].resources.requests.memory,NODE:.spec.nodeName' \
  --field-selector spec.nodeName="$NODE",status.phase=Running --sort-by=.metadata.namespace

Requests, not usage — this is what the scheduler reserved, which is what makes a node "full" while top looks idle. status.phase=Running leaves out finished jobs, which reserve nothing.

docs.title: Reproducible container digest in CI
docs.text:
# Never deploy a tag. Tags move; digests do not.
DIGEST=$(docker buildx imagetools inspect "$IMAGE:$TAG" --format '{{json .Manifest}}' | jq -r .digest)
kubectl set image deploy/app "app=$IMAGE@$DIGEST"

For a multi-architecture image this is the digest of the index, so each node still pulls its own architecture.

docs.title: Network forensics
docs.text:
Who is listening, who is talking, and where packets die. All of these are in the base install or one package away.

Tested on Ubuntu 24.04 with iproute2 ss, OpenBSD netcat, iputils ping, mtr 0.95 and tcpdump 4.99.

docs.title: What is listening, and which process owns it?
docs.text:
sudo ss -tulpn

The modern netstat -tulpn: TCP and UDP, listening sockets, process names, no DNS lookups. netstat comes from net-tools, which most distributions no longer install by default; ss reads the kernel directly and is faster on busy hosts.

docs.title: Which remote addresses hold the most connections?
docs.text:
ss -Htn state established | awk '{print $4}' \
  | sed -E 's/:[0-9]+$//; s/^\[::ffff:(.*)\]$/\1/' \
  | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head

One address with hundreds of connections is either your load balancer or the thing you are looking for.

docs.title: Which process is talking to this address?
docs.text: sudo ss -tnp dst 203.0.113.10

docs.title: Is the port reachable from here?
docs.text:
nc -zv -w 3 db.internal 5432

-z connects without sending data, -w 3 gives up after three seconds. "Timed out" usually means a firewall drops the packets; "connection refused" means the host answered and nothing listens on the port.

docs.title: Is the path MTU smaller than it should be?
docs.text:
# 1472 bytes of payload + 28 bytes of headers = 1500. Do not fragment.
ping -c 5 -M do -s 1472 example.com

If this fails while a normal ping works, something on the path has a smaller MTU and drops large packets: the classic "SSH connects, then hangs" or "small requests work, big ones time out". Lower -s until it passes to find the real size.

docs.title: Where along the path are packets lost?
docs.text:
mtr -rwbzc 100 example.com

Report mode (-r), wide output, IPs and AS numbers, 100 probes. Loss that starts at one hop and continues to the end is real; loss on one middle hop only is that router deprioritising replies to probes, and can be ignored.

docs.title: Capture only new connection attempts
docs.text:
# SYN packets without ACK: every new TCP connection, nothing else.
sudo tcpdump -nni any 'tcp[tcpflags] & (tcp-syn|tcp-ack) == tcp-syn'

Small enough to leave running during an incident. Add -w syn.pcap to keep it for Wireshark.

docs.title: nftables
docs.text: Tested with nftables 1.0.9 and systemd 255 on Ubuntu 24.04, on a host that also runs Kubernetes (k3s) rules.

docs.title: Default-deny that does not lock you out
docs.text:
Set up the revert first, then load. If the new rules cut your SSH session, the timer removes them two minutes later.

# 1. Arm the revert: in 120 s, delete the table this ruleset creates.
sudo systemd-run --unit=nft-revert --on-active=120 --timer-property=AccuracySec=1s \
  nft delete table inet filter

# 2. Validate, then load. `nft -c` parses without applying.
sudo nft -c -f /etc/nftables.conf && sudo nft -f /etc/nftables.conf

# 3. Still connected? Cancel the revert.
sudo systemctl stop nft-revert.timer

Delete only the table you added. nft flush ruleset as a revert also deletes Docker's and Kubernetes' rules, and restoring a saved copy of the whole ruleset fails on those (unsupported xtables compat expression). If your /etc/nftables.conf begins with flush ruleset, it has the same effect when you load it, so on container hosts start it with table inet filter and flush table inet filter instead.

docs.title: PostgreSQL
docs.text: Tested on PostgreSQL 16. The column names below are for PostgreSQL 13 and later.

docs.title: Find the unindexed query before adding cache
docs.text:
SELECT calls, round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 1) AS avg_ms,
       round(total_exec_time::numeric) AS total_ms, query
  FROM pg_stat_statements
 WHERE query NOT ILIKE '%pg_stat%'
 ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC
 LIMIT 15;

Sort by total time, not mean. A 4ms query run 900k times beats a 2s query run twice, and only one of them is worth your afternoon.

It needs one-time setup, or it fails with "pg_stat_statements must be loaded via shared_preload_libraries":

# postgresql.conf, then restart PostgreSQL:
#   shared_preload_libraries = 'pg_stat_statements'
sudo -u postgres psql -c 'CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_stat_statements;'

docs.title: strace
docs.text:
strace is on every box and needs no kernel support, but it stops the process on every syscall it traces. Run it on one host for seconds, not on the fleet. For anything hot, use BPF instead.

Tested with strace 6.8 on Ubuntu 24.04. -p takes a comma-separated list, so pgrep -d, attaches to every matching worker at once.

docs.title: Which files does this service open most?
docs.text:
Good for finding filter candidates before you turn on verbose auditing.

sudo timeout 60s strace -f -qq -e trace=openat -p "$(pgrep -d, -f php-fpm)" 2>&1 \
  | sed -nE 's/.*openat\(.*"([^"]+)".*/\1/p' \
  | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -30

docs.title: Where does its time go?
docs.text:
# Syscall summary: count, errors and time per syscall. Prints on exit.
sudo timeout -s INT 30s strace -c -f -qq -p "$PID"

-s INT matters: strace prints the summary when interrupted, the same as pressing Ctrl-C.

docs.title: Only the slow calls
docs.text:
# Syscalls that took longer than 100 ms, with timestamps.
sudo timeout 60s strace -f -qq -e signal=none -tt -T -p "$PID" 2>&1 \
  | awk -F'<' 'NF > 1 && $NF + 0 > 0.1'

-T appends the time spent in each call as <0.301288>; the awk keeps lines over the threshold. Expect wait4 and sleeps in the output — they are slow on purpose.

docs.title: Only the calls that fail
docs.text:
# Every file-related syscall that returned an error.
sudo timeout 30s strace -f -qq -e signal=none -e trace=%file -e status=failed -p "$PID"

The fastest way to find a missing config file, a wrong path or a permission error that the application swallows.

docs.title: systemd
docs.text: Tested with systemd 255 on Ubuntu 24.04.

docs.title: A unit that actually restarts on failure
docs.text:
[Unit]
# Without this, repeated crashes hit the start limit (5 starts in 10 s) and
# systemd gives up: the unit sits in "failed" until someone looks.
StartLimitIntervalSec=0

[Service]
Restart=always
RestartSec=2
TimeoutStopSec=30

StartLimitIntervalSec must be in [Unit]. In [Service] systemd ignores it and the limit stays at 10 seconds: in a test, the unit gave up after 5 restarts with the line in [Service], and kept restarting with it in [Unit]. Check what is actually in effect:

systemctl show myapp -p StartLimitIntervalUSec -p StartLimitBurst

docs.title: How exposed is each service?
docs.text:
systemd-analyze security                 # every service, scored 0 (locked down) to 10
systemd-analyze security ssh.service     # one service, every setting explained

Most distribution units score "UNSAFE" or "EXPOSED". The per-service view lists the hardening options (ProtectSystem=, NoNewPrivileges=, PrivateTmp= …) that would lower the score; add them in a drop-in with systemctl edit, one at a time, and restart to check nothing breaks.
